sentences.text: The Rodrigues starling, scientifically named Necropsar rodericanus, was an extinct passerine bird belonging to the Sturnidae family.
This species was endemic to Rodrigues Island, which is part of the Mascarene archipelago in the southwest Indian Ocean.
The bird measured between 25 and 30 centimeters in length, a size considered large for a starling.
Its plumage was white or whitish-grey, contrasting with dark brown wings, while its legs and beak were yellow.
Although the skull was similar in size to that of the hoopoe starling, the overall skeleton was smaller.
The only known sighting of the living bird occurred when French sailor Julien Tafforet was marooned on the island between 1725 and 1726.
Historical accounts describe the bird eating eggs and dead tortoises, which it tore apart using its powerful beak.
Descriptions from the time indicate the bird possessed a complex song.
Subfossil bones of the bird were first discovered by George Jenner in 1866 and 1871, and later by Henry H. Slater in 1874.
The genus Necropsar was formally named by Günther and Newton in 1879.
Robust limbs and strong jaws indicate that the bird foraged for food on the ground.
The bird likely used its wedge-shaped bill to open entrances and remove objects while searching for food, similar to other starlings and crows.
Its feeding adaptations support historical observations that the bird ate eggs and dead tortoises.
Its diet could have consisted of various snails and other invertebrates of Rodrigues, as well as carrion.
Although capable of flight, the bird had a smaller sternum than other starlings, suggesting it did not require powerful flight due to the island's small size and topography.
It lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
The species was extinct by the time of the 1761 French Transit of Venus expedition.
Tafforet observed that the bird lived on the islet of Gombrani located south of Rodrigues.
It was debated by Masauji Hachisuka whether the subfossils described by Günther and Newton belonged to the bird reported by Tafforet, based on differences in diet and crest presence.
Conversely, Günther and Newton considered the species likely identical to the bird described by Tafforet due to its strongly built bill.
It is debated whether the bird was sexually dimorphic due to insufficient fossil remains.
In 1967, ornithologist James Greenway suggested the bird should belong to the same genus as the Réunion starling, Fregilupus, due to similarities between the two species.
In 1974, additional subfossils increased support for the hypothesis that the Rodrigues starling was a distinct genus.
